tip: 께 (kke) is the honorific 'to' – it replaces 에게 (ege) when the receiver deserves respect: 어른들께 (eoreundeulkke) = to the elders.
드리다 (deurida) is the humble 'give' aimed upward at elders – so the bow is offered: 정성껏 드려요 (jeongseongkkeot deuryeoyo). To a friend you'd 주다 (juda) instead.
-고 (-go) links the two actions in order: 세배를 하고 (sebaereul hago) = do the bow, and then 세뱃돈을 받아요 (sebaetdoneul badayo) = you receive the money.
께서 (kkeseo) marks an honored subject; the verb takes 주셨어요 (jusyeosseoyo).
Korean normally avoids stating others' feelings directly – 기쁘다 (gippeuda = glad) becomes 기뻐하다 (gippeohada = show gladness) for other people: 아이들이 기뻐해요 (aideuri gippeohaeyo).
팔리다 (pallida) = get sold – it's 팔다 (palda = sell) with -리- (-ri-) making it happen to the tickets: 다 팔렸어요 (da pallyeosseoyo) = all sold out.
A number + -이나 (-ina) marks the amount as a lot: 다섯 시간이나 (daseot siganina) = a whole five hours. Without it, the trip simply took five hours.
새해 복 많이 받으세요 (saehae bok mani badeuseyo) = the set New Year greeting.
-대요 (-daeyo) reports what people say: 낳는대요 (nanneundaeyo) = they say one will have a baby.
햇- (haet-) before a food means this year's first harvest: 햇곡식으로 (haetgoksigeuro) = with the new grain, 햇감자 (haetgamja) = new potatoes. One syllable marks freshness.
보름달 (boreumdal) = the full moon; Chuseok falls on a full-moon night.
Dates use Sino-Korean numbers: 오월 팔일 (owol paril) = May 8, literally 'five-month eight-day'. Native numbers like 다섯 (daseot) are not used for the date itself.
달아 드려요 (dara deuryeoyo): -아/어 드리다 (deurida) turns an action into a humble favor for an elder – pin it on for them. With friends the ending is -아/어 주다 (juda).
모시다 (mosida) = to accompany an elder respectfully; 모시고 (mosigo) = escorting them.
감사드리는 (gamsadeurineun) is the humble form of thanking - used for someone above you, like a teacher.
웃으셨어요 (useusyeosseoyo) = smiled; the honorific -(으)시- and the past tense fuse into the 셨 you see here, marking respect for the teacher.
찾아뵈어요 (chajaboeeoyo) is the humble word for visiting someone senior, not the everyday 만나요 (mannayo).
생각나요 (saenggangnayo) means the memory comes up by itself – the old teacher surfaces in your mind rather than you doing the remembering.
미역국 (miyeokguk) = seaweed soup, eaten on birthdays and after childbirth.
생일 축하해요 (saengil chukahaeyo) is literally 'I congratulate your birthday' – 축하하다 (chukahada) is a verb, so Korean congratulates the day rather than wishing it happy.
환갑 (hwangap) marks 예순 살 (yesun sal), the 60th birthday – one full cycle of the traditional 60-year calendar, which is why it gets its own name and a big family celebration.
-마다 (-mada) glues 'every' straight onto a noun: 생일마다 (saengil-mada) = every birthday. No separate word needed – the noun itself carries it.
돌잡이 (doljabi) = the baby grabs an object to foretell its future.
In 돌잡이 (doljabi) the grabbed object foretells the future: 연필 (yeonpil) = a scholar's path.
Korean normally avoids stating someone else's feelings directly – 온 가족이 기뻐해요 (on gajogi gippeohaeyo) uses -어하다 (-eohada) = shows happiness. Plain 기뻐요 (gippeoyo) is for your own joy.
떠나서 (tteonaseo) folds 'because' into the verb with -서 (-seo) – the reason comes first and the result follows: my friend leaves, so I'm sad.
화가 나다 (hwaga nada) = to get angry: the anger 화 (hwa) is what rises, so it takes the subject marker 가 (ga).
친구가 부러워요 (chinguga bureowoyo) marks the friend with 가 (ga) as the subject – 부럽다 (bureopda) works like 'is enviable', so the envied person is the subject, not an object.
긴장돼요 (ginjangdwaeyo) is built on 되다 (doeda = become), so the nerves are something that happens to you. 되 (doe) + 어 (eo) fuses into the 돼 (dwae) you see here.
